lessons.title: The European cybersecurity landscape
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a circle of yellow stars around a shield, linked by lines to several small watch stations.
objectives: Place the European actors: Commission, ENISA, national authorities, CSIRTs.
Describe the cooperation networks: NIS Cooperation Group, CSIRTs network, EU-CyCLONe.
Explain the European cybersecurity certification framework.
Name the mechanisms of the Cyber Solidarity Act.

references.title: Regulation (EU) 2019/881 on ENISA and on cybersecurity certification (Cybersecurity Act)
Directive (EU) 2022/2555 (NIS 2), Articles 14 to 16: Cooperation Group, CSIRTs network, EU-CyCLONe
Regulation (EU) 2025/38 on cyber solidarity, in force since February 4, 2025

blocks.text: Why a European approach?

Networks, suppliers and attacks ignore borders. An outage in one country's energy or health sector can affect its neighbors. The European Union therefore sets common rules and organizes cooperation between Member States, which remain responsible for their national security.

rows: Proposes legislation, adopts implementing acts, funds programs
Advises, prepares certification schemes, supports cooperation and crisis management
Supervise entities and impose penalties (for example ANSSI in France)
Receive incident notifications and help with response

blocks.text: Three cooperation networks (NIS 2)

blocks.title: From strategic to operational
blocks.alt: Three-level diagram: the NIS Cooperation Group, which brings together the Member States, the Commission and ENISA for strategic guidance; EU-CyCLONe, which coordinates the management of large-scale crises and incidents; the CSIRTs network, which exchanges technical information and coordinates response.

blocks.text: The Cybersecurity Act (2019/881)

This regulation gives ENISA a permanent mandate and creates a European cybersecurity certification framework for ICT products, services and processes. A certificate issued under a European scheme is recognized throughout the Union. The schemes provide three assurance levels: basic, substantial and high. The first scheme adopted, EUCC, is based on the Common Criteria.

blocks.title: European cybersecurity certification (certification européenne de cybersécurité)
blocks.text: Attestation, under a scheme adopted at EU level, that an ICT product, service or process meets security requirements for a given assurance level (basic, substantial or high).
The Cyber Solidarity Act (2025/38)

rows: National and cross-border cybersecurity hubs that detect threats and share alerts
Preparedness (testing of critical sectors), EU reserve of trusted providers, mutual assistance
ENISA analyzes a significant or large-scale incident and draws recommendations from it

blocks.title: Dates to check
blocks.text: Texts verified on November 17, 2026; some obligations apply in stages: check the consolidated version on EUR-Lex before citing a date.
In the exam: ENISA = advice, certification, cooperation; it does not penalize companies. National authorities supervise and impose penalties.

blocks.title: SOC case: an incident that crosses the border
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: a fictitious managed service provider, present in three countries, suffers a compromise in the lab. The SOC prepares the notification to the national CSIRT of its country of establishment. The trainer shows how the information then flows through the CSIRTs network and, if the crisis spreads, to EU-CyCLONe.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: identifies the competent authority and the CSIRT to which the organization must report.
SOC manager: keeps the national CSIRT's contact details and the notification format close at hand.
Auditor: checks that the organization knows the texts that apply to it.
Risk manager: follows the arrival of new texts and their application dates.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: ENISA advises and coordinates; it does not impose penalties.
EU-CyCLONe manages crises; the CSIRTs network handles technical cooperation.
The assurance levels of European certification: basic, substantial, high.
The Cyber Solidarity Act does not replace NIS 2: it adds detection, a reserve and mutual assistance.
The EU sets common rules; the Member States supervise and impose penalties.
ENISA: permanent mandate since Regulation 2019/881.
Cooperation Group, CSIRTs network, EU-CyCLONe.
European certification: three assurance levels; EUCC based on the Common Criteria.
Cyber solidarity: alert, emergency, incident review.

lessons.title: The main texts: NIS 2, DORA, CRA and CER
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of four binders of different colors side by side, each marked with a European star.
objectives: Describe the scope of NIS 2: essential and important entities.
Explain what DORA requires of the financial sector.
Describe the obligations of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) for digital products.
Place the CER Directive, the GDPR and the AI Act within this whole.

references.title: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for the financial sector (DORA)
Directive (EU) 2022/2557 on the resilience of critical entities (CER)

blocks.text: A family of complementary texts

rows: Risk management, incident notification, management accountability
Transposition by October 17, 2024, applicable since October 18, 2024
Financial sector and its critical ICT providers
Security by design and throughout the support period
Reporting from September 11, 2026; most of it on December 11, 2027

blocks.text: NIS 2: who is covered?

NIS 2 applies, as a general rule, to medium and large companies in the sectors listed in its annexes. Annex I covers sectors of high criticality: energy, transport, banking, financial market infrastructures, health, drinking water, waste water, digital infrastructure, ICT service management (business-to-business), public administration, space. Annex II covers other critical sectors: postal services, waste management, chemicals, food, manufacturing, digital providers, research. Some entities are covered regardless of their size (for example DNS service providers or qualified trust service providers).

blocks.title: Essential or important entity
blocks.text: Essential entities (generally the large entities in Annex I sectors) are subject to ex ante and ex post supervision. Important entities are subject to lighter, ex post supervision. The security obligations are the same; supervision and the maximum fines differ.
DORA: resilience of the financial sector

blocks.title: The pillars of DORA
blocks.alt: Five-pillar diagram: ICT risk management under the responsibility of the management body; management, classification and reporting of major incidents; resilience testing, including threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for the entities concerned; management of ICT third-party risk and oversight of critical providers; sharing of threat information.

blocks.title: DORA and NIS 2
blocks.text: For financial entities, DORA is the specific text: its requirements take precedence over those of NIS 2 for ICT risk management and incident reporting.
The CRA: products secure by default

The Cyber Resilience Act imposes essential requirements on manufacturers of products with digital elements (software, connected devices): security by design, no known exploitable vulnerability when placed on the market, secure configuration by default, security updates during the support period, in principle of at least five years. Compliant products bear the CE marking. Manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents through a single platform managed by ENISA.
And the other texts?

rows: Security of personal data, breach notification to the authority within 72 hours
Robustness and cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems
Critical entities within the meaning of CER are treated as essential entities under NIS 2

blocks.text: Remember the target of each text: NIS 2 = organizations in critical sectors; DORA = finance; CRA = products; CER = resilience of critical entities; GDPR = personal data.

blocks.title: SOC case: which text applies?
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: the trainer presents three fictitious SOC clients: a medium-sized hospital, a bank and a manufacturer of connected cameras. The analyst links the first to NIS 2 (health), the second to DORA, the third to the CRA for its products, and points out that the GDPR applies to all three as soon as they process personal data.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: draws up the list of applicable texts and assigns each one to an owner.
SOC manager: aligns notification procedures with each text's deadlines.
Auditor: checks the entity's classification (essential or important) and its justification.
Risk manager: integrates regulatory compliance into the risk map.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: NIS 2 is a directive: it is transposed into national law. DORA and the CRA are regulations: they apply directly.
Essential and important entities have the same security obligations; supervision and fines differ.
For finance, DORA takes precedence over NIS 2 for ICT risk.
The CRA targets products, not the organization that uses them.
NIS 2: critical sectors, essential and important entities.
DORA: ICT risk, incidents, tests, providers, sharing.
CRA: security of digital products, CE marking, reporting to ENISA.
CER, GDPR and the AI Act complete the whole.
Texts verified on November 17, 2026; some obligations apply in stages: check the consolidated version on EUR-Lex before citing a date.

lessons.title: Operational requirements in practice
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a clock marked 24 h and 72 h next to a checklist of ten boxes.
objectives: List the ten categories of measures in Article 21 of NIS 2.
Apply the NIS 2 notification deadlines and compare them with those of the GDPR and the CRA.
Organize supply chain security and vulnerability management.
Prepare the evidence expected by the supervisory authority.

references.title: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690: technical requirements for certain digital entities

blocks.text: The ten minimum measures (Article 21 of NIS 2)
Entities must take technical, operational and organizational measures proportionate to the risks, following an "all-hazards" approach. Article 21 sets at least the following measures.

rows: Policies on risk analysis and information system security
Business continuity: backups, disaster recovery, crisis management
Security in acquisition, development and maintenance, including vulnerability handling and disclosure
Assessment of the effectiveness of the measures
Human resources security, access control, asset management
Multi-factor or continuous authentication, secured communications, including emergency communications

blocks.text: Reporting a significant incident

blocks.title: The NIS 2 deadlines (Article 23)
blocks.alt: Four-step timeline: early warning to the CSIRT or the authority within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident; incident notification within 72 hours, with an initial assessment; intermediate report if the authority requests it; final report no later than one month after the notification.

rows: Early warning within 24 h, notification within 72 h
72 h to the supervisory authority, unless the risk is unlikely
Actively exploited vulnerability or severe incident affecting a product
Early warning within 24 h through the ENISA platform
Deadlines set by technical standards: to be checked

blocks.title: One incident, several notifications
blocks.text: An intrusion with theft of personal data at a NIS 2 entity may require one notification to the CSIRT (NIS 2) and another to the data protection authority (GDPR). The response procedure must provide for both channels and their deadlines.
Supply chain and vulnerabilities

blocks.title: Putting it into practice
items: Keep an inventory of critical suppliers and assess their security; write it into contracts (incident notification, audit, end of contract).
Publish a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and a point of contact.
Track vulnerabilities in the products used and apply patches according to their criticality.
Roll out multi-factor authentication for sensitive and remote access.
Test backups and crisis plans, and keep a record of these tests.

blocks.title: Oversee suppliers and development
items: Classify suppliers by criticality and scale due diligence (questionnaire, certification, audit).
Monitor their access and require prompt notification of their incidents.
Plan the exit from the contract onward: data return, reversibility, access removal.
Require secure development and change control from internal teams and vendors alike.
Keep patch discipline: deadlines set by severity, exceptions approved and tracked.

blocks.title: Proof of compliance
blocks.text: The authority expects verifiable elements: approved policies, risk analyzes, test reports, incident registers, proof of training, supplier contracts. A measure without a written record is hard to demonstrate.
Deadlines are classic traps: NIS 2 = 24 h / 72 h / 1 month; GDPR = 72 h. The deadline runs from the moment the entity becomes aware of the incident.

blocks.title: SOC case: the countdown
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: at 10 a.m., the SOC of a fictitious entity confirms a significant intrusion in the lab. The analyst starts the regulatory timer: early warning before 10 a.m. the next day, notification before 10 a.m. three days later. The analyst also informs the data protection officer, because fictitious personal data is involved.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: has senior management approve the policies that cover the ten measures.
SOC manager: builds the regulatory deadlines into escalation procedures and ticketing tools.
Auditor: asks for evidence of each measure and the incident registers.
Risk manager: assesses dependence on critical suppliers and their security level.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: The NIS 2 early warning is due within 24 h; the full notification within 72 h.
The NIS 2 final report arrives no later than one month after the notification.
The supply chain is part of the minimum measures (point d).
The GDPR and NIS 2 can apply to the same incident.
Article 21: ten categories of measures, all-hazards approach.
Article 23: 24 h, 72 h, one month.
GDPR: 72 h; CRA: 24 h for exploited vulnerabilities.
Suppliers, vulnerabilities, multi-factor, tests: with written evidence.

lessons.title: Mapping to CISSO and the frameworks
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of two columns of boxes linked by crossing arrows, like a mapping table.
objectives: Link the NIS 2 measures to the CISSO domains studied in this course.
Use ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF 2.0 to demonstrate compliance.
Build a mapping matrix that avoids duplicate work.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security management systems: requirements

blocks.text: One system, several requirements

An organization has no interest in creating a different program for each text. It relies on a management system (often ISO/IEC 27001) and links each regulatory requirement to the measures that already address it. CISSO knowledge covers most of these measures.

blocks.title: Regulation or framework?
blocks.text: A regulatory text (NIS 2, DORA, GDPR) sets obligations and expected outcomes, backed by penalties: it says what. A framework (ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF) organizes implementation and evidence: it helps say how. Each obligation is mapped to controls, owners and processes.

blocks.title: Building a mapping matrix
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: list the requirements of each applicable text; link them to the existing measures of the management system; spot the gaps; address the gaps and gather the evidence only once for several texts.

blocks.title: Certification is not compliance
blocks.text: Being ISO/IEC 27001 certified helps a lot, but does not on its own prove compliance with NIS 2: the certified scope, the notification deadlines and management accountability must be checked separately.

blocks.title: ENISA and NIST complement, they do not replace
blocks.text: ENISA guidance (measures, maturity, European good practice) and NIST publications (risk, controls, incident response) help with implementation. They never replace the legal obligation: in an inspection, the European text and its national transposition prevail. Done well, mapping avoids duplicated controls and reports, and reveals gaps in owners, evidence or testing.
"One management system, one matrix, shared evidence."
NIST CSF 2.0 added the Govern function to the five historical functions (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). It fits well with the management accountability required by NIS 2.

blocks.title: SOC case: one piece of evidence for two requirements
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: the lab team prepares a fictitious audit. The SOC's incident register serves as evidence both for NIS 2 incident handling and for the corresponding ISO/IEC 27001 control. The analyst adds to the register the time the incident became known, which is essential to demonstrate that deadlines were met.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: the matrix avoids multiplying programs and shows senior management the coverage.
SOC manager: SOC registers and metrics are evidence for several texts.
Auditor: checks that each requirement has a measure and evidence.
Risk manager: addresses gaps according to risk and possible penalties.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: An ISO/IEC 27001 certification does not mean automatic compliance with NIS 2.
CSF 2.0: six functions, including Govern.
The matrix links requirements, measures and evidence; it does not replace risk analysis.
The NIS 2 measures overlap with the CISSO domains.
ISO/IEC 27001 and NIST CSF 2.0 serve as the backbone.
Matrix: list, link, spot gaps, share evidence.

lessons.title: Penalties and the role of management
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a meeting table with a judge's gavel on it and a chart showing a rising arrow.
objectives: Explain the obligations of management bodies under NIS 2.
Name the maximum fines under NIS 2 and the GDPR.
Describe how these texts change the role of the CISO and senior management.

blocks.text: Management becomes accountable

NIS 2 places cybersecurity at management level. Management bodies must approve the risk management measures, oversee their implementation and can be held liable for failures. Their members must follow training, and the entity is encouraged to offer it regularly to its staff. DORA goes in the same direction for the financial sector: the management body bears ultimate responsibility for ICT risk.

blocks.title: What management must do
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: approve the risk management measures; oversee their implementation; get trained to understand the risks; be held accountable for failures.

blocks.text: The fines

rows: At least €10 million or 2% of total worldwide annual turnover
At least €7 million or 1.4% of total worldwide annual turnover
€20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual turnover

blocks.text: For NIS 2, these amounts are minimum ceilings that each Member State must at least provide for in its transposition law. For an essential entity, the authority may also, as a last resort, suspend a certification or temporarily prohibit an executive from exercising management functions.
What changes for the CISO

blocks.title: The new role
items: Report regularly to senior management, with understandable metrics.
Have policies and risk decisions formally approved, and keep a record of them.
Organize training for executives.
Prepare the relationship with the supervisory authority: contacts, evidence, notifications.
Take part in decisions on critical suppliers and budgets.

rows: Tracked metrics, recorded exceptions, corrective actions
Review schedule and reporting to management

blocks.title: Ready for the auditor or the authority
items: Accurate, protected and easily retrievable evidence.
Risk register, audit results and supplier records kept up to date.
Incident logs, recovery test reports and board reporting.
Risk acceptances approved by management and regular reviews of residual risk.
During an incident: severity, owners and notification routes defined, legal and privacy involved, decisions recorded.

blocks.title: Not just fear of the fine
blocks.text: Penalties give the CISO weight, but the goal remains resilience: senior management that understands the risks decides better and faster during a crisis.
A defensible security officer translates technical findings into business impact, presents options and exceptions, gets decisions made, and proves continuous improvement.
In the exam: NIS 2 = €10 million or 2% (essential), €7 million or 1.4% (important); GDPR = up to €20 million or 4%. Management accountability is Article 20 of NIS 2.

blocks.title: SOC case: preparing the management briefing
blocks.text: Simulated exercise: after a fictitious quarter, the SOC manager prepares a one-page summary for the executive committee: number of significant incidents, notification deadlines met, critical patches overdue, result of the last crisis exercise. Senior management approves a budget for multi-factor authentication on remote access.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: becomes an advisor to senior management, not just a technician.
SOC manager: SOC metrics feed the management dashboard.
Auditor: checks the approval minutes and the proof of executive training.
Risk manager: translates cyber risks into financial and regulatory impact.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Executives approve and oversee; they can be held liable.
The NIS 2 ceilings are minimums that the Member States must provide for.
The temporary ban on management functions applies to essential entities, as a last resort.
The highest GDPR fines go up to 4% of worldwide turnover.
NIS 2, Article 20: approve, oversee, get trained, answer for failures.
Fines: €10 million / 2% and €7 million / 1.4% (NIS 2); up to €20 million / 4% (GDPR).
The CISO reports to senior management, with evidence and metrics.
Texts verified on November 17, 2026; some obligations apply in stages: check the consolidated version on EUR-Lex before citing a date.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: European governance and compliance
Actors: Commission (texts), ENISA (advice, certification, cooperation), national authorities (supervision, sanctions), CSIRTs (incidents).
NIS 2 networks: Cooperation Group (strategy), CSIRTs network (technical), EU-CyCLONe (crises).

NIS 2 (Directive 2022/2555): transposition October 17, 2024, applies from October 18, 2024; essential and important entities.
DORA (Regulation 2022/2554): finance, since January 17, 2025; ICT risk, incidents, testing (TLPT at least every 3 years), third-party providers, sharing.
CRA (Regulation 2024/2847): digital products; reporting from September 11, 2026, most obligations on December 11, 2027.
CER (Directive 2022/2557): resilience of critical entities; GDPR: personal data; Regulation 2024/1689: AI.
Article 21: ten measures (risk, incidents, continuity, suppliers, development and vulnerabilities, effectiveness, hygiene and training, cryptography, HR and access, multifactor).
Article 23: early warning 24 h, notification 72 h, final report one month later. GDPR: 72 h.

Article 20: management approves, oversees, gets trained, answers for failures.

questions.prompt: What is the role of ENISA?
questions.explanation: ENISA advises, prepares the certification schemes and supports cooperation; it does not impose sanctions.

whyNot.0: It is the Parliament and the Council that adopt the texts.
whyNot.2: It supports their network without replacing them.
whyNot.3: National authorities are the ones that impose sanctions.

questions.prompt: Which network coordinates the management of large-scale cyber crises in the EU?
questions.explanation: EU-CyCLONe connects the member states' cyber crisis management authorities.

whyNot.0: It oversees the application of the GDPR.
whyNot.2: It handles technical cooperation.

questions.prompt: What are the assurance levels of European cybersecurity certification?
choices: Divisions D, C, B, then A
questions.explanation: Regulation 2019/881 provides for three assurance levels.

whyNot.2: These are not regulatory levels.
whyNot.3: Those are the Common Criteria levels.

questions.prompt: What does Regulation (EU) 2025/38 on cyber solidarity create?
choices: An alert system and a reserve of service providers
An obligation to encrypt all data
questions.explanation: It creates a European alert system, an emergency mechanism with a reserve of trusted providers, and a review of incidents.

whyNot.1: It does not impose general encryption.
whyNot.2: That is the purpose of the GDPR.
whyNot.3: That is the purpose of the CRA.

questions.prompt: Who supervises and sanctions the entities subject to NIS 2?
questions.explanation: Each state designates its competent authorities, which supervise and impose sanctions.

whyNot.1: They cooperate but do not supervise foreign entities.
whyNot.2: It does not directly supervise the entities.

questions.prompt: Which text targets the cybersecurity of entities in critical sectors such as energy and health?
questions.explanation: NIS 2 covers the sectors listed in its Annexes I and II.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an important entity from an essential entity under NIS 2?
questions.explanation: The measures are the same; supervision (after the fact) and the fine ceiling differ.

whyNot.3: They must also notify significant incidents.

questions.prompt: Since when has the DORA regulation applied?
questions.explanation: DORA has applied since January 17, 2025.

whyNot.0: That is the main application date of the CRA.
whyNot.1: That is the application date of NIS 2.
whyNot.2: That is the application date of the GDPR.

questions.prompt: A bank is subject to both NIS 2 and DORA. Which text prevails for ICT risk management?
choices: The CRA, the text on products
questions.explanation: DORA is the sector-specific act: its requirements prevail for ICT risk and incidents.

whyNot.2: NIS 2 actually predates the application of DORA; what matters is specificity.

questions.prompt: What must a manufacturer guarantee under the Cyber Resilience Act?
choices: Security updates during the support period
A SOC open day and night
An ISO/IEC 27001 audit of its customers
questions.explanation: The CRA requires security by design and security updates during the support period.

whyNot.2: It does not require a SOC.

questions.prompt: Under NIS 2, within what time frame must the early warning of a significant incident be sent?
questions.explanation: Early warning within 24 h, notification within 72 h, final report one month later.

whyNot.2: This deadline does not exist in NIS 2.

questions.prompt: When must the NIS 2 final report be submitted?
choices: Only if the authority asks for it
One week after the early warning
questions.explanation: Article 23 sets a final report no later than one month after the incident notification.

whyNot.1: It is the intermediate report that is submitted on request.
whyNot.2: This deadline is not provided for.

questions.prompt: An intrusion steals personal data at a NIS 2 entity. What should be done?
choices: Wait until the internal investigation is fully complete
Notify only the national CSIRT, within 24 hours
Warn only the customers whose data leaked
Notify the CSIRT and the data protection authority
questions.explanation: Both texts apply: each has its own channel and deadlines (24/72 h and 72 h).

whyNot.0: The deadlines run from the moment you become aware of the incident.
whyNot.1: The GDPR also requires its own notification.
whyNot.2: The authority must be notified, and the individuals if the risk is high.

questions.prompt: Which of these measures appears explicitly in Article 21 of NIS 2?
questions.explanation: Point (d) covers supply chain security.

whyNot.0: No audit frequency is set in this way.
whyNot.3: No certification of this kind is imposed.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer discovers that a flaw in its product is being actively exploited. What does the CRA require?
choices: An annual declaration to the Commission
An early warning within 24 hours through ENISA
Just a fix in the next release
No reporting if a fix exists
questions.explanation: The CRA requires actively exploited vulnerabilities to be reported, through ENISA's single reporting platform.

whyNot.2: Reporting is mandatory and fast.

questions.prompt: Which function did NIST CSF 2.0 add?
questions.explanation: CSF 2.0 (2024) adds Govern to the five original functions.

whyNot.2: It already existed.

questions.prompt: Why build a mapping matrix between texts and measures?
choices: To share measures and evidence across requirements
questions.explanation: The same measure and the same evidence can meet several requirements.

whyNot.2: No certification is automatic.

questions.prompt: Is an ISO/IEC 27001 certified entity automatically compliant with NIS 2?
choices: No, the scope and specific requirements must be checked
No, ISO/IEC 27001 is incompatible with NIS 2
Yes, if the certification is less than three years old
questions.explanation: Certification helps a lot, but the scope, notification deadlines and management liability are checked separately.

whyNot.1: On the contrary, it is a good foundation.
whyNot.2: The date changes nothing.

questions.prompt: Which CISSO domain does the NIS 2 measure "business continuity and crisis management" correspond to?
questions.explanation: Point (c) of Article 21 covers backups, disaster recovery and crisis management.

whyNot.0: It falls under the all-hazards approach, but not under this point.

questions.prompt: What must management bodies do under Article 20 of NIS 2?
choices: Carry out the penetration tests themselves
Delegate all security to the CISO
questions.explanation: They approve the measures, oversee their implementation, receive training and can be held liable.

whyNot.2: Article 20 does not require it.

questions.prompt: What is the fine ceiling for an essential entity under NIS 2?
questions.explanation: Whichever amount is higher applies; states can provide for more.

whyNot.0: This amount does not exist in NIS 2.
whyNot.1: That is the highest GDPR ceiling.
whyNot.2: That is the ceiling for important entities.

questions.prompt: Which obligation does NIS 2 impose on members of management bodies?
choices: Being on call for the SOC
questions.explanation: Article 20 requires training to understand and assess risks.

whyNot.2: It is not required.

questions.prompt: Which last-resort measure does NIS 2 allow against an essential entity?
questions.explanation: As a last resort, the authority can temporarily ban an executive from exercising management functions.

whyNot.0: NIS 2 does not provide for it.
whyNot.1: It is not a NIS 2 measure.
whyNot.3: That makes no legal sense here.

questions.prompt: Which change does NIS 2 bring most to the CISO's role?
questions.explanation: Management becomes accountable: the CISO advises it, keeps it informed and has decisions approved.

whyNot.1: The CISO continues to run them.
whyNot.2: The two roles remain separate.

questions.prompt: What is the legal difference between NIS 2 and DORA?
choices: DORA is transposed, NIS 2 applies directly
NIS 2 is transposed, DORA applies directly
questions.explanation: A directive is transposed into national law; a regulation applies as is.

whyNot.2: It is the other way around.
